For years, I believed that American healthcare was the best in the world. I am
embarrassed by how readily I accepted that claim. Perhaps I, too, was
susceptible to that familiar American malady of exceptionalism.

At the Yale School of Public Health, I am the director of the Center for
Infectious Disease Modeling and Analysis and hold an endowed chair in
epidemiology. My research evaluates the effectiveness and cost efficiency of
public health policies in the United States and around the world. Yet I had
not sufficiently questioned this premise about my own country.

Over three decades of research across dozens of countries, the evidence
gradually unsettled that conviction. Nations with far fewer resources were
providing care to everyone, often achieving better outcomes while spending
much less. Patients see a doctor, receive treatment, and go home. No
deductibles. No invoice in the mail. The cost was shared collectively, much as
we fund public schools and fire departments.

Why were we unable to do the same? And what would it take to change that?
